questions.text: Which combination best captures the chapter's discussion of living organisms?
options: Metabolism, cellular organisation and response to stimuli among a combination of features
questions.explanation: No single feature such as growth or reproduction alone defines life; the chapter stresses a combination of characteristics.

questions.text: Growth in living organisms is described as an increase in:
questions.explanation: Growth is commonly described as increase in mass and increase in number.

questions.text: Why is growth not an exclusive defining feature of living organisms?
options: Crystals can increase in size by external deposition
questions.explanation: Crystals can grow by deposition of material from outside, so growth alone does not distinguish living from non-living.

questions.text: In living organisms, growth generally occurs:
questions.explanation: Living growth generally occurs from within through internal processes.

questions.text: Which is the strongest reason reproduction cannot be the sole defining feature of life?
options: Some living organisms or individuals do not reproduce
questions.explanation: Reproduction is not universal among living organisms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example commonly used to show that reproduction is not universal?
questions.explanation: Mules are typically sterile and are a standard example in this context.

questions.text: Which set contains examples used to illustrate non-reproduction in living individuals?
options: Mule, sterile worker bee, infertile human
Bacteria, all fertile animals, all seeds
questions.explanation: These examples show that not every living individual reproduces.

questions.text: Metabolism refers to:
options: The sum total of chemical reactions in a living body
questions.explanation: Metabolism includes the totality of chemical reactions in an organism.

questions.text: Anabolism is best described as:
questions.explanation: Anabolism builds more complex molecules, for example during protein synthesis.

questions.text: Catabolism is best described as:
questions.explanation: Catabolic reactions break molecules down, as in glucose breakdown during respiration.

questions.text: Protein synthesis is an example of:
questions.explanation: Protein synthesis builds a complex molecule from smaller components.

questions.text: The breakdown of glucose during respiration is an example of:
questions.explanation: Glucose breakdown is a catabolic process.

questions.text: Why is metabolism especially important in defining living organisms in this chapter?
options: It is the sum of chemical reactions characteristic of living systems
questions.explanation: The chapter highlights metabolism as a defining feature of living organisms.

questions.text: A reaction performed in vitro is:
options: A reaction carried out outside a living body under laboratory conditions
questions.explanation: A reaction outside the living body may mimic a biochemical reaction but is not itself a living organism.

questions.text: Which statement about an isolated biochemical reaction is most appropriate?
options: It is itself a complete living organism
It cannot occur outside a body
An isolated reaction in vitro does not by itself constitute a living organism
questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes chemical reactions from the organised living system.

questions.text: The basic structural and functional unit of life is the:
questions.explanation: Cells provide the basic structural and functional organisation of living organisms.

questions.text: A unicellular organism is one that:
questions.explanation: Unicellular organisms carry out life processes within one cell.

questions.text: Multicellular organisms are characterised by:
options: Many cells with organisation and often division of labour
questions.explanation: Multicellular organisms have many cells arranged in an organised system.

questions.text: Responsiveness to environmental stimuli is associated with:
options: Consciousness in the broad biological sense used in the chapter
questions.explanation: Living organisms can sense and respond to environmental changes.

questions.text: Folding of Mimosa pudica leaves after touch illustrates:
questions.explanation: Touch is a stimulus and leaf folding is the response.

questions.text: A plant bending toward light is an example of:
questions.explanation: Light acts as an environmental stimulus to which the plant responds.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes movement from locomotion?
options: They always mean exactly the same thing
Movement can occur without an organism moving from place to place
questions.explanation: Plants can show movement without locomotion from one place to another.

questions.text: Which statement about motility is correct?
options: Some living organisms are sessile and do not move from place to place
Motility is the same as scientific naming
questions.explanation: Sessile organisms remain fixed in one place, so motility is not universal.

questions.text: Which is NOT a sound conclusion from the chapter?
options: Growth alone does not define life
Metabolism is important in defining living organisms
questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly gives exceptions to reproduction.

questions.text: Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Anabolism builds molecules, catabolism breaks them down.

questions.text: Which set contains only life-characteristic concepts discussed in this section?
options: Growth, reproduction, metabolism, cellular organisation, response to stimuli
questions.explanation: These are the principal characteristics discussed in the opening section.

questions.text: Biodiversity refers to:
questions.explanation: Biodiversity refers broadly to the variety of life.

questions.text: Identification in taxonomy means:
options: Recognising an organism and determining its identity
Preserving a plant on a sheet
questions.explanation: Identification establishes what organism is being studied.

questions.text: Nomenclature is the process of:
questions.explanation: Nomenclature is the assignment of scientific names.

questions.text: Classification is the process of:
options: Arranging organisms into groups based on similarities and differences
questions.explanation: Classification organises organisms into groups.

questions.text: The three basic activities of taxonomy are:
questions.explanation: These are the three core activities of taxonomy in the chapter.

questions.text: Systematics studies:
options: Diversity and relationships among organisms, including evolutionary relationships
questions.explanation: Systematics considers diversity and relationships, including evolutionary history.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes systematics from simply assigning names?
options: Systematics considers relationships as well as diversity
Systematics is another word for herbarium
questions.explanation: Systematics includes relationships among organisms, not just naming.

questions.text: Why are scientific names useful?
options: They are different in every village
They reduce confusion from different common names and standardise communication
They describe only an organism's colour
questions.explanation: Scientific names provide standardised communication across languages and regions.

questions.text: Which is NOT one of the three basic activities of taxonomy?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is a biological process, not a core taxonomic activity.

questions.text: Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Nomenclature concerns scientific naming.

questions.text: Which pairing is correct?
options: Classification—grouping organisms by similarities and differences
questions.explanation: Classification groups organisms using shared and distinguishing features.

questions.text: The term biodiversity is most directly concerned with:
options: Only the order of taxonomic ranks
questions.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the variety of living organisms.

questions.text: A researcher recognises an unknown plant using diagnostic features. This activity is:
questions.explanation: Recognising and determining identity is identification.

questions.text: A researcher assigns a formal scientific name to a species. This is:
questions.explanation: Assigning a scientific name is nomenclature.

questions.text: A researcher places organisms into groups according to shared characteristics. This is:
questions.explanation: Grouping organisms based on similarities and differences is classification.

questions.text: Which statement is most accurate?
options: Taxonomy's basic activities include identification, nomenclature and classification
questions.explanation: This is the core set of taxonomic activities.

questions.text: Which sequence is arranged from broadest to most specific?
options: Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
questions.explanation: This is the standard taxonomic hierarchy from broad to specific.

questions.text: Which is the most specific principal category in the hierarchy listed in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Species is the basic and most specific principal category in this hierarchy.

questions.text: Which category comes immediately below Kingdom in the animal hierarchy?
questions.explanation: The animal hierarchy proceeds Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

questions.text: Which category comes immediately above Genus?
questions.explanation: Family contains related genera.

questions.text: Which category comes immediately below Family?
questions.explanation: Genus is below family and above species.

questions.text: A taxonomic category refers to:
options: The rank or level in the hierarchy
questions.explanation: Category is the rank, such as family, genus or species.

questions.text: A taxon refers to:
options: A group or unit placed at any taxonomic rank
questions.explanation: A taxon is an actual group at a rank.

questions.text: Which example correctly distinguishes category from taxon?
options: Family is a category; a particular family is a taxon
A taxon is always a rank; category is an organism
questions.explanation: The category is the level; the taxon is the specific group occupying it.

questions.text: A genus generally comprises:
questions.explanation: A genus groups closely related species.

questions.text: A family generally comprises:
questions.explanation: A family groups related genera.

questions.text: An order generally comprises:
questions.explanation: An order groups related families.

questions.text: A class generally comprises:
questions.explanation: A class groups related orders.

questions.text: A phylum or division generally comprises:
questions.explanation: Phylum/division groups related classes.

questions.text: Kingdom is the broad category that groups related:
questions.explanation: Kingdom includes related phyla or divisions.

questions.text: Which term is commonly used for the plant category corresponding to animal phylum?
questions.explanation: Division is commonly used in plant classification; phylum is common in animals.

questions.text: Which sequence is ordered from specific to broader categories?
questions.explanation: Moving from species upward, each category is broader.

questions.text: If two species are placed in the same genus, this indicates that they are grouped as:
questions.explanation: A genus groups related species; same genus does not mean same species.

questions.text: Which statement about the hierarchy is correct?
options: Every rank contains only one taxon worldwide
Higher categories generally include more diverse groups
questions.explanation: Higher ranks are broader and include more diverse groups.

questions.text: Which order is correct between Class and Species?
questions.explanation: The hierarchy between class and species is order, family, genus, species.

questions.text: Which of the following is a taxonomic category rather than a particular named group?
questions.explanation: Genus is a rank/category; Homo is a particular genus taxon.

questions.text: Binomial nomenclature gives each species a name made of:
questions.explanation: A binomial consists of two parts: genus and specific epithet.

questions.text: In Homo sapiens, Homo is the:
questions.explanation: Homo is the genus name.

questions.text: In Homo sapiens, sapiens is the:
questions.explanation: Sapiens is the specific epithet.

questions.text: Which scientific name is formatted correctly?
questions.explanation: The genus begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a lowercase letter.

questions.text: Which word in a binomial begins with a capital letter?
questions.explanation: The genus name is capitalised.

questions.text: Which word in a binomial begins with a lowercase letter?
questions.explanation: The specific epithet begins with a lowercase letter.

questions.text: In printed text, scientific names are generally:
questions.explanation: Printed scientific names are italicised.

questions.text: When writing a scientific name by hand, the two parts are conventionally:
questions.explanation: When handwritten, each word is underlined separately.

questions.text: Which is the correctly written scientific name of the housefly from the chapter discussion?
questions.explanation: The genus Musca is capitalised and domestica is lowercase.

questions.text: In Mangifera indica, the word Mangifera is:
questions.explanation: Mangifera is the genus name.

questions.text: In Mangifera indica, indica is:
questions.explanation: Indica is the specific epithet.

questions.text: Which is the best explanation for using binomial nomenclature?
options: Every language has the same common names
It creates a standard two-part scientific name
questions.explanation: The system standardises scientific naming with two components.

questions.text: Which is incorrect under standard binomial formatting?
questions.explanation: The genus name should begin with a capital letter.

questions.text: Which formatting rule applies to both Homo sapiens and Mangifera indica in printed text?
questions.explanation: Both parts of a printed scientific name are italicised.

questions.text: Which statement is correct about the specific epithet?
options: It is always a complete species name by itself
It follows the genus name and begins with a lowercase letter
It is written first and capitalised
It is the same thing as taxonomic category
questions.explanation: The specific epithet is the second part of the binomial.

questions.text: A herbarium is primarily a collection of:
options: Dried, pressed and preserved plant specimens
questions.explanation: Herbarium specimens are preserved plant samples mounted on sheets.

questions.text: Which sequence best describes herbarium specimen preparation?
options: Collect, dry, press, preserve/mount and label
questions.explanation: Plant specimens are collected, dried, pressed, mounted and labelled.

questions.text: Which information may appear on a herbarium label?
options: Scientific name, family, locality, date and collector
questions.explanation: Labels record identification and collection details.

questions.text: A botanical garden mainly maintains:
questions.explanation: Botanical gardens grow and maintain living plants for study and reference.

questions.text: Which is a botanical garden example discussed in our notes?
questions.explanation: Kew is a well-known botanical garden.

questions.text: The Indian Botanical Garden mentioned in the notes is located at:
questions.explanation: The Indian Botanical Garden at Howrah is a standard example.

questions.text: Museums are useful in taxonomy because they:
options: Preserve and display specimens for study
questions.explanation: Museums maintain preserved specimens for reference and study.

questions.text: Larger animal specimens in museums may be:
questions.explanation: Larger animals may be stuffed for preservation and display.

questions.text: Insects in museum collections are commonly:
questions.explanation: Insects are often pinned and mounted.

questions.text: A zoological park is most directly associated with:
options: Living wild animals under human care
A list of plants in a region
questions.explanation: Zoological parks allow observation of living animals and their behaviour.

questions.text: Which aid is most useful for observing the behaviour of living wild animals?
questions.explanation: Animals can be observed alive in zoological parks.

questions.text: A taxonomic key identifies organisms using:
questions.explanation: Keys guide identification by contrasting character choices.

questions.text: A couplet in a taxonomic key consists of:
questions.explanation: A couplet contains two contrasting alternatives.

questions.text: A lead in a taxonomic key is:
options: Each individual statement in a couplet
questions.explanation: Each individual statement is called a lead.

questions.text: Flora generally provides information about:
options: Only one taxon in great detail
questions.explanation: A flora is an account of the plants of a region.

questions.text: A manual is useful because it helps:
questions.explanation: Manuals help users identify species and learn their names.

questions.text: A monograph is best described as:
options: A detailed account of one taxon
A list of only common names
questions.explanation: A monograph treats one taxon in detail.

questions.text: A catalogue is:
options: An organised list of organisms or taxonomic information
questions.explanation: A catalogue is an organised listing.

questions.text: Which match is incorrect?
questions.explanation: A pair of contrasting statements is a couplet in a key; a monograph is a detailed account of one taxon.

questions.text: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.explanation: Flora covers the plants of a particular region.

questions.text: Which aid is best matched with the purpose 'detailed account of a single taxon'?
questions.explanation: A monograph focuses in detail on one taxon.

questions.text: Which aid is best matched with the purpose 'identification using contrasting character pairs'?
questions.explanation: Taxonomic keys use contrasting characters.

questions.text: Which aid is best matched with the purpose 'living collection of plants'?
questions.explanation: Botanical gardens maintain living plants.

questions.text: Which aid is best matched with the purpose 'preserved specimens for study'?
questions.explanation: Museums preserve specimens.

questions.text: Which statement about taxonomical aids is most accurate?
options: Every aid performs exactly the same function
Different aids support complementary aspects of identification and study
questions.explanation: Different aids provide different kinds of evidence and reference.

questions.text: A student claims that a crystal is living because it increases in size. Which concept directly challenges this claim?
options: Growth can occur by external deposition in non-living crystals
questions.explanation: Crystal growth shows why growth alone is insufficient as a defining criterion.

questions.text: An infertile individual is still alive. Which inference is best supported?
options: Reproduction is not universal among living individuals
questions.explanation: The inability to reproduce does not mean an individual is non-living.

questions.text: A biochemical reaction is performed in a test tube. Why is the test tube reaction not itself a living organism?
options: It lacks the complete organisation of a living system
questions.explanation: An isolated in-vitro reaction is not a whole living organism.

questions.text: A plant responds to light but remains rooted in one place. Which pair of concepts does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Plants respond to stimuli and can move without locomoting from place to place.

questions.text: Which of the following is a definition-to-term match?
questions.explanation: Nomenclature is scientific naming; category is rank, taxon is the group, and couplet is a pair of statements.

questions.text: A biologist studies evolutionary relationships among organisms. Which field is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: Systematics includes diversity and relationships, including evolutionary history.

questions.text: Two statements in a key offer contrasting choices for identification. Together they form a:
questions.explanation: A pair of contrasting statements is a couplet.

questions.text: A student records that a plant specimen was collected at a specific place on a specific date by a named collector. Where would this information typically be recorded?
questions.explanation: Herbarium labels commonly record collection locality, date, collector and taxonomic details.

questions.text: A reference work gives a detailed treatment of a single genus. Which kind of aid does this most closely resemble?
questions.explanation: A monograph gives a detailed account of one taxon; a genus can be the taxon treated.

questions.text: A reference listing organims in an organised format is most likely a:
questions.explanation: A catalogue is an organised list of organisms or taxonomic information.

questions.text: Which pair contains one taxonomic activity and one taxonomical aid?
questions.explanation: Classification is a taxonomic activity; a herbarium is a taxonomical aid.

questions.text: Which sequence correctly matches the three concepts?
questions.explanation: These definitions distinguish the three basic activities of taxonomy.

questions.text: Which is the best example of a common-name problem that scientific nomenclature helps solve?
options: The same organism may have different local names in different places
All organisms have identical names worldwide
Every species belongs to the same genus
questions.explanation: Standard scientific names reduce ambiguity caused by local/common names.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a taxonomical aid listed in our chapter notes?
questions.explanation: Catabolism is a metabolic process, not a taxonomical aid.

questions.text: A student says 'Family is a taxon and category in exactly the same sense.' Which correction is best?
options: Family is a category/rank; a particular family is a taxon at that rank
Family is not part of taxonomy
questions.explanation: Category is the rank, while a specific group occupying that rank is a taxon.

questions.text: Which fact is an exception rather than a universal rule for living organisms?
options: All living organisms carry out metabolism
questions.explanation: Reproduction is not universal; sterile individuals are examples.

questions.text: Which statement best captures why multiple characteristics are considered when identifying life?
options: Each individual characteristic is always unique to life
Some characteristics, such as growth or reproduction, have exceptions
questions.explanation: Growth can occur in crystals and reproduction is not universal, so multiple features are considered.

questions.text: Which of the following changes a broad grouping into a more specific grouping as you move down the hierarchy?
questions.explanation: Moving down from kingdom toward species gives increasingly specific categories.

questions.text: A plant is identified by choosing between paired contrasting character statements. What is the method being used?
questions.explanation: The taxonomic key uses contrasting characters in couplets.

questions.text: Which option contains only examples of taxonomical aids or taxonomic reference resources?
questions.explanation: Herbaria, botanical gardens, museums and keys are taxonomical aids.

questions.text: Which statement is most accurate about the word 'species' in the chapter's hierarchy?
options: It is the most specific principal category listed
It is the same as a couplet
questions.explanation: Species is the most specific principal rank in the hierarchy presented.

questions.text: If a scientific name is printed as 'mangifera Indica', what is the formatting error?
options: Genus is lowercase and specific epithet is capitalised
questions.explanation: The genus should be capitalised and the specific epithet lowercase: Mangifera indica.

questions.text: Which of the following names follows the genus-capital/specific-epithet-lowercase convention?
questions.explanation: Musca is capitalised and domestica is lowercase.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly identifies the taxonomic level above Order?
questions.explanation: Class is above order; the sequence is Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species.

questions.text: Which level sits between Phylum/Division and Order?
questions.explanation: Class follows phylum/division and precedes order.

questions.text: Which level sits between Order and Genus?
questions.explanation: Family is between order and genus.

questions.text: A herbarium differs from a botanical garden because a herbarium contains:
options: Preserved plant specimens rather than a collection of living plants
questions.explanation: Herbaria preserve plant specimens; botanical gardens maintain living plants.

questions.text: A zoological park differs from a museum because a zoological park primarily contains:
questions.explanation: Zoological parks allow study of living animals.

questions.text: Which is the most appropriate role for a flora?
options: Providing a pair of contrasting statements
questions.explanation: Flora records the plants of a particular region.

questions.text: A guide helps a user determine the identity and name of a species in a region. Which aid is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: A manual supports identification and naming of species.

questions.text: Which term refers to one statement within a taxonomic key?
questions.explanation: A lead is an individual statement; a couplet is a pair.

questions.text: Which term refers to the pair of alternatives within a taxonomic key?
questions.explanation: A couplet contains two contrasting statements.

questions.text: Which option best distinguishes a monograph from a catalogue?
options: Monograph gives a detailed account of one taxon; catalogue is an organised list
Monograph is living plants; catalogue is preserved animals
Catalogue uses only contrasting character pairs
questions.explanation: These reference resources have different scopes and functions.

questions.text: Which of the following is an incorrect association?
questions.explanation: Grouping by similarities and differences is classification; nomenclature is naming.

questions.text: Which is the correct association?
options: Systematics—only the study of one herbarium sheet
questions.explanation: Classification groups organisms; nomenclature names them; identification establishes identity.

questions.text: Which option best explains the relationship between taxonomy and taxonomical aids?
options: Taxonomy is supported by aids such as keys, herbaria and manuals
Taxonomy is the same as a zoological park
Aids remove the need for identification
questions.explanation: Taxonomical aids provide material and references to support identification and study.

questions.text: Which of these is a direct example of response to stimuli?
questions.explanation: Mimosa leaf folding is a response to touch.

questions.text: Which statement about crystals is relevant to the definition of life?
options: Crystal growth demonstrates that growth alone is not sufficient to define life
questions.explanation: Crystals can grow through external deposition, which is why growth alone is not decisive.

questions.text: Which is the best interpretation of 'living growth from within' in the chapter?
options: Internal biological processes contribute to growth
Every non-living object grows from within
Growth is the same as locomotion
questions.explanation: Living growth is associated with internal processes rather than simple external deposition.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is false?
options: A monograph treats one taxon in detail
A flora concerns plants of a region
A couplet is a pair of contrasting statements
A lead is a pair of contrasting statements
questions.explanation: A lead is one statement; a couplet is the pair.
